title: Design an ATM Machine
summary: Two problems in one. A state machine for the card-to-cash flow, and a note-dispensing algorithm where greedy is wrong often enough to matter — and knowing exactly when is the whole interview.

evidence.title: Amazon interview experience — SDE-1, 3.5 years
evidence.note: Round 5, hiring manager. One of three system design questions in that round.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: Interviewers use this because it has a clean split. The **flow** — card in, PIN, select, dispense, card out — is a state machine, and it is graded the same way the vending machine is. The **dispense** is a coin-change problem where the greedy answer is wrong for some inputs, and noticing that is what separates candidates.

An ATM holds notes in a fixed set of denominations. A customer inserts a card, authenticates, chooses withdraw or deposit, and the machine dispenses notes or accepts them. It must never dispense more than it holds, never dispense the wrong amount, and never debit an account without dispensing.

items.title: Which denominations, and how many of each?
items.text: LeetCode 2241 fixes them at 20, 50, 100, 200, 500 with unlimited counts per denomination but a finite stock. Real machines are 10/20/50. The counts matter more than the values.

items.title: Largest-notes-first, or fewest notes?
items.text: For a canonical set these are the same. For an arbitrary set they are not — and that is the follow-up.

items.title: Is the account balance checked here or by a bank service?
items.text: Say the ATM calls a `BankService`. It keeps the design honest and gives you a seam for the failure cases.

items.title: What happens if dispensing fails halfway?
items.text: The interesting one. A debit followed by a jam is the failure everyone remembers. It is why the debit comes *after* the notes are staged.

items.title: Card retention after three wrong PINs?
items.text: A small rule, but it is a state, and getting it into the diagram shows you are modelling the real thing.

blocks.text: The flow is a state machine

blocks.title: Card in to card out
blocks.caption: The card is ejected on every terminal path — including failure. An ATM that keeps your card because of an exception is a headline, not a bug.
blocks.code:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> CardInserted : insertCard()
    CardInserted --> Authenticated : correct PIN
    CardInserted --> CardInserted : wrong PIN (attempts < 3)
    CardInserted --> CardRetained : wrong PIN x3
    Authenticated --> SelectingAmount : chooses Withdraw
    SelectingAmount --> Dispensing : amount ok, notes available
    SelectingAmount --> Authenticated : rejected, retry
    Dispensing --> Idle : notes out, card ejected
    Authenticated --> Idle : cancel / eject card
    CardRetained --> Idle : operator reset

blocks.title: Order of operations is the correctness argument
blocks.text: **Reserve the notes, debit the account, then release.** Debit-then-dispense means a jam has taken the customer's money. Dispense-then-debit means a crash has given money away. Reserving first makes the failure recoverable: if the debit fails you return the notes to the hopper and nothing happened.
LeetCode 2241 says *largest denomination first*. That is a stated rule, not an optimisation — and it is worth knowing that the rule and the optimum can disagree.

blocks.title: Greedy is not always optimal, and you should say when
blocks.text: For **canonical** systems (10/20/50/100, or 1/5/10/25) largest-first uses the fewest notes. For an arbitrary set it can fail outright: with denominations {1, 3, 4} and a target of 6, greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 = three notes when 3 + 3 = two is correct. LeetCode 2241 *mandates* largest-first, so greedy is required there — but naming the limitation is what gets you the follow-up credit.

blocks.filename: Fewest notes, when greedy is not allowed

blocks.title: Three collaborators, one state
blocks.caption: The ATM owns the flow. Cash, accounts and cards are three separate concerns, and the bank being an interface is what lets you test the failure paths.
blocks.code:
classDiagram
    class ATM {
        -State state
        -CashDispenser dispenser
        -BankService bank
        -Card current
        -int pinAttempts
        +void insertCard(Card c)
        +void enterPin(String pin)
        +void withdraw(int amount)
        +void ejectCard()
    }
    class CashDispenser {
        -int[] denominations
        -int[] counts
        +Optional~int[]~ plan(int amount)
        +void commit(int[] take)
    }
    class BankService {
        <<interface>>
        +boolean authenticate(Card c, String pin)
        +Money balanceOf(Account a)
        +boolean debit(Account a, Money m)
    }
    class State {
        <<interface>>
        +void enterPin(ATM a, String pin)
        +void withdraw(ATM a, int amount)
        +void ejectCard(ATM a)
    }
    ATM --> State
    ATM o-- CashDispenser
    ATM --> BankService

items.title: Fewest notes instead of largest-first
items.text: Bounded coin-change DP, above. Name the complexity — O(amount × denominations) — and note it is pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial.

items.title: Deposits
items.text: Notes go in, counts go up, and the account is credited. The mirror-image failure applies: credit only after the notes are physically accepted.

items.title: Concurrency across many ATMs on one account
items.text: Two withdrawals racing on the same balance. The debit must be a conditional update — `UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount` — not read-then-write.

items.title: Daily withdrawal limits
items.text: Belongs on the bank service, not the ATM. Putting the rule in the machine means twelve machines with twelve opinions.

items.title: Audit and reconciliation
items.text: Every dispense is a ledger entry. The physical note count must reconcile against the ledger, and disagreement is the alarm.

items.title: Out of a denomination mid-day
items.text: `plan` already handles it by returning empty. The interesting part is telling the customer *before* they enter an amount that cannot be made.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: Amount not expressible in available notes — e.g. £30 with only £50s → refuse before touching the hopper.
Amount exceeds the balance → bank rejects; the ATM never learns the balance unless it asks.
Amount exceeds total cash in the machine → refuse early, and do not leak how much is inside.
Wrong PIN three times → retain the card, and make sure the *state* enforces it rather than a counter someone can forget to reset.
Cancel at any point before dispensing → card ejected, nothing debited.
Zero or negative amount → rejected at validation, not at the dispenser.

rows: A state machine, with card retention as a state
Reserves, debits, releases — and explains why
One pass, mutates as it goes
Plans first, commits only if exact
Names canonical sets, and the {1,3,4} counterexample
Bank is an interface; limits live there

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–5** clarify denominations, counts, and who owns the balance. **5–12** state machine on the board, including card retention. **12–22** code the dispenser's plan/commit split. **22–30** the reserve-debit-release ordering and what each failure does. **30–38** greedy versus DP, with the counterexample. **38–45** concurrency across machines.
